message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"9ed6f63d93c278ff8ed41240ad72e7f24da9d14ee10605b5810e3f28a96cf41e","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nv-class-c:lineage:56","source_registry_sha256":"3e184808e042e052d0c78d0dff47c50b34a56560f428649c492afe10bc7ba712","units":[{"unit_id":"sec05-u01","module_id":"sec05-m01","objective_ids":["sec05-u01"],"title":{"text":"Who must yield","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Not yielding when required is the top cause of crashes in Nevada, so these rules prevent more crashes than almost any others.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02"]},{"text":"Knowing the order at intersections removes the guesswork that leads to collisions.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]},{"text":"Driveways and side roads are where many drivers forget that they, not main-road traffic, must give way.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-R02"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"You reach an intersection with no signs or signals at the same moment as a car on your right.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03"]},"reasoning":{"text":"At an intersection with no signs or signals, the vehicle on your right should usually go first.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-R01"]},"result":{"text":"You let the car on your right go first, then proceed with caution.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking the law gives a driver the right-of-way, so that driver can simply go.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02"]},"correction":{"text":"The law only says who must yield, and even a driver who may legally go first must do everything possible to avoid a crash.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Already in goes first; straight beats left; driveways wait.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-F06"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"You are leaving a shopping center driveway onto a main road where a pedestrian is crossing and cars are coming. Who goes first?","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-R02"]},"answer":{"text":"The pedestrian and the main-road traffic.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06"]},"rationale":{"text":"Drivers entering a main road from a driveway or private road must yield to all main-road traffic and to pedestrians.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-R02"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Sharing the right-of-way","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"The top cause of crashes.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02"]},{"text":"The law names who yields.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson is about who must yield. Not yielding when required is the top cause of crashes in Nevada, and the yielding rules depend on courtesy, common sense and cooperation. Nevada law does not hand anyone the right-of-way. It only says who has to yield, and even a driver who legally may go first must do everything possible to avoid a crash. We will cover intersections without signs, vehicles already in the intersection, left turns, driveways, four-way stops, emergency vehicles, freeway entry, cyclists, funerals and pedestrians.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":34,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Intersection order","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"No signs or signals: right usually first.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]},{"text":"Already in the intersection goes first.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]},{"text":"Straight traffic before left turns.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"At an intersection with no signs or signals, the vehicle on your right should usually go first. A vehicle that is already in the intersection goes before vehicles that are only now arriving. A vehicle going straight that is already in the intersection has priority over a vehicle turning left; the left-turner may go once it has yielded and signalled. Together these rules settle most situations at an uncontrolled intersection: first, who is already there; then, between arriving vehicles, the one on the right; and for turns, straight traffic first.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Driveways and four-way stops","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Driveway or minor road: yield to all.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-F08"]},{"text":"Four-way stop: first to arrive goes first.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-F08"]},{"text":"Always after a complete stop.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Drivers coming onto a main road from a minor road, a private road or a driveway must yield to all traffic on the main road and to pedestrians. At a four-way stop, the driver who reached the intersection first goes first, after a complete stop. So the four-way stop has its own order based on arrival, not on who is on the right. The driveway rule is the strictest of all: the driver entering from a driveway gives way to everyone already using the main road, including people walking across the entrance. Arrival order rules there.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Emergency vehicles and processions","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Emergency vehicle from any direction: pull right.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-F11"]},{"text":"Stay out of intersections; stop until it passes.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-F11"]},{"text":"Let a funeral procession pass together.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"When an emergency vehicle using its siren or flashing lights approaches from any direction, pull over at once to the right edge, staying out of any intersection, and wait stopped until it goes by. That applies even when the emergency vehicle is on the other side of the road. Yield to a funeral procession too, and let the vehicles with their headlights on pass together as one group rather than cutting into the line. In both cases you give up your place so that a group with a special purpose can move without interruption.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Pedestrians","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Crosswalks and intersections: yield to pedestrians.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]},{"text":"Pedestrians still check both ways.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]},{"text":"Cane or guide dog: always yield.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"Vehicles must give way to pedestrians in crosswalks and at intersections, yet before stepping off the curb pedestrians should make sure cars in both directions have stopped. A blind or visually impaired person on foot who uses a guide dog or other service animal, or carries a white cane or walking stick, has the right-of-way. Drivers must yield, stop fully if needed and take care before going on. That rule comes from state law, and it protects people who may not be able to see your vehicle coming at all. Look both ways at every crossing.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s6","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Two different orders","fact_ids":["sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-F03","sec05-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Uncontrolled: vehicle on the right.","fact_ids":["sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-F03","sec05-F08"]},{"text":"Four-way stop: first to arrive.","fact_ids":["sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-F03","sec05-F08"]},{"text":"Left-turners and driveways yield.","fact_ids":["sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-F03","sec05-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap with two orders. At an uncontrolled intersection, the vehicle on the right usually goes first, but at a four-way stop the order is set by who arrived and stopped first. Using the wrong rule at the wrong intersection is a common error. A second trap involves two yielding drivers: a left-turning driver yields to straight-through traffic already in the intersection, and a driver leaving a driveway or private road yields to everything on the main road, pedestrians included. Check the type of intersection first, then apply its rule.","fact_ids":["sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-F03","sec05-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check a driveway exit","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Leaving a shopping center driveway.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-R02"]},{"text":"A pedestrian and cars coming.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-R02"]},{"text":"Who goes first?","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are leaving a shopping center driveway onto a main road. A pedestrian is crossing the driveway entrance, and cars are coming along the main road. Who goes first? Decide before reading on. The pedestrian and the main-road traffic both go first. Drivers coming onto a main road from a driveway or private road must yield to all traffic on the main road and to pedestrians. You wait until the pedestrian has passed and there is a safe gap in traffic, then pull out. Being ready to go does not give you the right-of-way.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Yielding recap","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F08","sec05-F07","sec05-F11","sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"The law only names who yields.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F08","sec05-F07","sec05-F11","sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]},{"text":"Freeway traffic and cyclists go first.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F08","sec05-F07","sec05-F11","sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]},{"text":"Always yield to pedestrians.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F08","sec05-F07","sec05-F11","sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"To review, failing to yield is the top crash cause in Nevada, and the law only says who must yield. At an uncontrolled intersection the vehicle on the right usually goes first, vehicles already in the intersection go before new arrivals, straight traffic goes before left turns, and driveway drivers yield to everyone. At a four-way stop the first to arrive goes first. Pull right and stop for emergency vehicles, let funerals pass, yield to freeway traffic when joining, yield to cyclists in bike lanes, and yield to pedestrians, always including a blind person with a cane or guide dog.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F08","sec05-F07","sec05-F11","sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec05-u02","module_id":"sec05-m02","objective_ids":["sec05-u02"],"title":{"text":"Speed and the Basic Rule","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-F15","sec05-R04"]},"why_how":[{"text":"The posted limit is not always a safe speed; Nevada's Basic Rule asks you to match your speed to conditions.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-F15"]},{"text":"Going too slowly can be as risky as going too fast, especially in the left lane.","fact_ids":["sec05-F19"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"On a highway posted at sixty-five miles per hour, a sudden snow squall cuts visibility and coats the road.","fact_ids":["sec05-F18","sec05-F15"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Limits are set for normal conditions, and the safe speed can be well below the limit when weather makes the road slick or hard to see.","fact_ids":["sec05-F18","sec05-F15","sec05-R04"]},"result":{"text":"The driver slows well below sixty-five until conditions improve.","fact_ids":["sec05-F18","sec05-F15"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking driving at the posted limit is always legal and safe.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-F15"]},"correction":{"text":"The limit is the upper bound for normal conditions; the Basic Rule can require a much lower speed.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-F14"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Limits are for good days; conditions set your speed.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A two-lane road in your direction has faster cars stacking up behind you. What should you do?","fact_ids":["sec05-F19"]},"answer":{"text":"Move to the right lane and let them pass.","fact_ids":["sec05-F19"]},"rationale":{"text":"Driving too slowly is unsafe too, and where two or more lanes run the same way, slower traffic must move right.","fact_ids":["sec05-F19"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Choosing a safe speed","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-F16","sec05-F20"]},"lines":[{"text":"The Basic Rule.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-F16","sec05-F20"]},{"text":"Example limits.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-F16","sec05-F20"]},{"text":"Speeding saves little.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-F16","sec05-F20"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson is about speed. Nevada has a Basic Rule that asks for a reasonable or proper speed, on top of whatever limit is posted. We will look at what the Basic Rule asks you to weigh, why the safe speed can be lower than the posted limit, the example speed limits the handbook gives for different kinds of roads, why driving too slowly can also be unsafe, and how little time speeding really saves. Speed is one of the few things a driver controls completely, so choosing it well is one of the most important skills in this chapter.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-F16","sec05-F20"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The Basic Rule","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-F15"]},"lines":[{"text":"Reasonable or proper speed.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-F15"]},{"text":"Weigh traffic, weather, sight and surface.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-F15"]},{"text":"Never a speed that endangers anyone.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-F15"]}],"narration":{"text":"Nevada's Basic Rule requires a reasonable or proper speed. On top of any posted limit, weigh the amount and type of traffic, the weather and how far you can see, the road surface, and whether the road is flat or steep, straight or curvy, wide or narrow. Never drive at a speed that puts yourself or anyone else in danger; depending on conditions, the safe speed may be well below the posted limit. So the limit is never permission to drive that fast in every situation; it is only the most you may drive when conditions are good.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-F15"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Example Nevada limits","fact_ids":["sec05-F16","sec05-F17","sec05-F18"]},"lines":[{"text":"School zones: fifteen miles per hour.","fact_ids":["sec05-F16","sec05-F17","sec05-F18"]},{"text":"Business and residential: twenty-five.","fact_ids":["sec05-F16","sec05-F17","sec05-F18"]},{"text":"Freeways: sixty-five; rural interstates: seventy plus.","fact_ids":["sec05-F16","sec05-F17","sec05-F18"]}],"narration":{"text":"The handbook gives example speed limits for Nevada roads. School zones are fifteen miles per hour, and business and residential areas, as well as school zones, can be twenty-five. Reduced-speed areas leading into towns are forty-five. Urban freeways and rural highways are sixty-five, and rural interstate freeways are seventy miles per hour or more. These are examples, not a replacement for the signs you see. Posted limits are set for normal driving conditions, so when bad weather cuts visibility or makes the road slick, lower your speed below the posted number.","fact_ids":["sec05-F16","sec05-F17","sec05-F18"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Too slow and too fast","fact_ids":["sec05-F19","sec05-F20","sec05-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Driving too slowly is unsafe too.","fact_ids":["sec05-F19","sec05-F20","sec05-R03"]},{"text":"Slower traffic keeps right.","fact_ids":["sec05-F19","sec05-F20","sec05-R03"]},{"text":"Speeding saves only seconds.","fact_ids":["sec05-F19","sec05-F20","sec05-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Driving too slowly is unsafe too, and where two or more lanes run in the same direction, slower traffic must move right and let others pass. At the other end, speeding saves very little time. Over five miles, driving seventy miles per hour instead of sixty saves only forty-three seconds. Covering fifteen miles at seventy rather than sixty saves just two minutes and nine seconds, and a ticket costs both time and money. When you weigh those small savings against the extra danger, there is little reason to drive faster than conditions allow.","fact_ids":["sec05-F19","sec05-F20","sec05-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Limit versus Basic Rule","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-F14","sec05-F15","sec05-F18"]},"lines":[{"text":"The limit is a ceiling.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-F14","sec05-F15","sec05-F18"]},{"text":"Conditions can lower it.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-F14","sec05-F15","sec05-F18"]},{"text":"Weather, traffic, sight, surface.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-F14","sec05-F15","sec05-F18"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Many drivers treat the posted limit as the right speed, as if driving at the limit were always legal. But the posted limit is the upper bound for normal conditions, while the Basic Rule can demand a much lower speed when traffic, weather, visibility or the road surface call for it. So a driver going exactly the limit in heavy fog can still be driving too fast for the conditions. When a question describes rain, snow, darkness or heavy traffic, the answer usually involves slowing below the posted number, not holding it.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-F14","sec05-F15","sec05-F18"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check slow traffic","fact_ids":["sec05-F19"]},"lines":[{"text":"Two lanes your direction.","fact_ids":["sec05-F19"]},{"text":"Cars stacking up behind.","fact_ids":["sec05-F19"]},{"text":"What do you do?","fact_ids":["sec05-F19"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are driving on a road with two lanes in your direction, and faster cars are stacking up behind you. What should you do? Recall the rule about slow traffic before reading on. Move to the right lane and let them pass. Driving too slowly is unsafe too, and where two or more lanes run in the same direction, slower traffic must move right. Staying in the left lane forces others to pass on the wrong side or to tailgate, which makes the road less safe for everyone, including you. Keep right when slower.","fact_ids":["sec05-F19"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Speed recap","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-F15","sec05-R04","sec05-F16","sec05-F17","sec05-F18","sec05-F19","sec05-F20","sec05-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"The Basic Rule sets a safe speed.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-F15","sec05-R04","sec05-F16","sec05-F17","sec05-F18","sec05-F19","sec05-F20","sec05-R03"]},{"text":"Example limits by road type.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-F15","sec05-R04","sec05-F16","sec05-F17","sec05-F18","sec05-F19","sec05-F20","sec05-R03"]},{"text":"Speeding saves only seconds.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-F15","sec05-R04","sec05-F16","sec05-F17","sec05-F18","sec05-F19","sec05-F20","sec05-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us sum up. Nevada's Basic Rule calls for a reasonable or proper speed that weighs traffic, weather, visibility, the road surface and the type of road, and the safe speed can be well below the posted limit. The handbook's example limits run from fifteen miles per hour in school zones and twenty-five in business and residential areas to forty-five near towns, sixty-five on urban freeways and rural highways, and seventy or more on rural interstates. Slow down in bad weather, keep right if you are slower, and remember that speeding saves only seconds or a couple of minutes.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-F15","sec05-R04","sec05-F16","sec05-F17","sec05-F18","sec05-F19","sec05-F20","sec05-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec05-u03","module_id":"sec05-m03","objective_ids":["sec05-u03"],"title":{"text":"Entering and driving freeways","fact_ids":["sec05-F21","sec05-F22","sec05-F23"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Freeways are usually the safest roads, but entering, merging and changing lanes at high speed need good habits.","fact_ids":["sec05-F21","sec05-F24"]},{"text":"Ramp meters control how cars join the freeway, and they work only if every driver follows them.","fact_ids":["sec05-F28"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"A driver on an on-ramp sees a gap in freeway traffic but is still well below freeway speed.","fact_ids":["sec05-F24"]},"reasoning":{"text":"In the acceleration lane, look for a gap, signal, and accelerate until close to freeway speed, avoiding a stop unless it cannot be helped.","fact_ids":["sec05-F24","sec05-R05"]},"result":{"text":"The driver signals and speeds up to match the flow before merging, rather than slowing or stopping.","fact_ids":["sec05-F24"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking it is safer to stop at the end of the on-ramp and wait for a big gap.","fact_ids":["sec05-F24"]},"correction":{"text":"Stopping before the merge makes a slow, dangerous entry into fast traffic; stop only if it cannot be helped.","fact_ids":["sec05-F24"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Find the gap, signal, match the speed.","fact_ids":["sec05-F24"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A ramp meter on your on-ramp is switched on and shows red. What do you do?","fact_ids":["sec05-F28"]},"answer":{"text":"Pull up to the stop line, stop, and wait for green.","fact_ids":["sec05-F28"]},"rationale":{"text":"When a ramp meter is on, stop on red at the stop line, expect quick changes, wait for green, then merge safely.","fact_ids":["sec05-F28"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Freeway basics","fact_ids":["sec05-F21","sec05-F24"]},"lines":[{"text":"Why freeways are safest.","fact_ids":["sec05-F21","sec05-F24"]},{"text":"Entering and merging.","fact_ids":["sec05-F21","sec05-F24"]},{"text":"Lanes and ramp meters.","fact_ids":["sec05-F21","sec05-F24"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers freeway driving. Freeways are usually the safest roads because access is limited, traffic flows one way without stopping, and drivers meet no intersections, signals, railroad crossings or sharp curves. Even so, high speeds leave less room for mistakes. We will look at planning a trip, entering by the on-ramp, merging smoothly, keeping with the flow of traffic, using the left lane properly, looking far ahead, changing lanes safely, and handling ramp meters. Good freeway habits are mostly about planning and smooth, predictable movement.","fact_ids":["sec05-F21","sec05-F24"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":34,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Before and at the ramp","fact_ids":["sec05-F22","sec05-F23"]},"lines":[{"text":"Plan the route and know your exits.","fact_ids":["sec05-F22","sec05-F23"]},{"text":"Check the gas gauge.","fact_ids":["sec05-F22","sec05-F23"]},{"text":"Enter only by the on-ramp.","fact_ids":["sec05-F22","sec05-F23"]}],"narration":{"text":"Before a freeway trip, plan the route, check a map if you are unsure of the way, know your entrances and exits, and check the gas gauge. Knowing your exits ahead of time lets you move over calmly instead of at the last moment. Enter a freeway by the on-ramp. Do Not Enter and Wrong Way signs tell a driver who has made a mistake, so if you see them, you are going the wrong way and must stop and correct course safely. A little planning before you set off prevents most of the trouble that happens near ramps. Plan first.","fact_ids":["sec05-F22","sec05-F23"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Merging","fact_ids":["sec05-F24","sec05-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Find a gap and signal.","fact_ids":["sec05-F24","sec05-R05"]},{"text":"Accelerate to near freeway speed.","fact_ids":["sec05-F24","sec05-R05"]},{"text":"Merging drivers yield.","fact_ids":["sec05-F24","sec05-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"In the merge or acceleration lane, look for a gap, signal, and accelerate until you are close to the freeway's speed. Avoid stopping before the merge unless it cannot be helped, because stopping makes a slow, dangerous entry into fast traffic. Merging drivers must yield to traffic already on the freeway, while drivers already on it should watch for merging cars and adjust speed so merges stay smooth. So both sides have a job: the merging driver matches speed and yields, and the through driver leaves room when it is safe to do so.","fact_ids":["sec05-F24","sec05-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Driving with the flow","fact_ids":["sec05-F25","sec05-F26","sec05-F27","sec05-R06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Keep with the flow of traffic.","fact_ids":["sec05-F25","sec05-F26","sec05-F27","sec05-R06"]},{"text":"Leave the far-left lane for faster traffic.","fact_ids":["sec05-F25","sec05-F26","sec05-F27","sec05-R06"]},{"text":"Look twenty to thirty seconds ahead.","fact_ids":["sec05-F25","sec05-F26","sec05-F27","sec05-R06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Freeway traffic often moves faster than traffic on other highways with the same posted limit, because there are fewer stop-and-go situations, so keep with the flow.
